n: The book opens by introducing Elkanah, a man from the hill country of Ephraim, with a short family tree. The great story of Samuel, Saul, and David begins in an ordinary household.

f.g: The full name of Ramah, Samuel's hometown, a few miles north of Jerusalem.
Here probably means an Ephraimite, someone living in Ephraim's territory; Chronicles lists the family among the Levites.

n: Elkanah has two wives. Peninnah has children, but Hannah has none. In that culture childlessness brought deep sorrow and social shame, and plural marriage often brought rivalry.

f.g: Means “grace” or “favor.”

n: Each year the family goes to Shiloh, where the tabernacle stood, to worship. The narrator quietly introduces Eli's sons, Hophni and Phinehas, who will matter later.

f.g: “Hosts” means armies — the Lord commands the armies of heaven and Israel. This is the first time the title appears in the Bible.
Israel's religious center in the time of the judges, where the tabernacle and ark rested.

n: At the sacrificial feast, Elkanah gives shares of the meat to Peninnah and each of her children. The many portions highlight how large her family is.

f.g: Shares of meat from a peace offering, which the worshippers ate together.

n: To Hannah he gives a special, generous portion because he loves her. Yet the Lord had not let her have children, and no amount of love from Elkanah could fill that ache.

f.g: The Hebrew is unclear; it may mean a double or choice portion.

n: Peninnah, Hannah's rival, taunts her cruelly about her childlessness to upset her.

f.g: rival; a co-wife who competes with her
irritated or taunted her severely

n: This pattern repeats every year at the very time of worship. Hannah ends up weeping and unable to eat, even at the feast.

f.g: The tabernacle at Shiloh, apparently with some permanent structures by this time.

n: Elkanah tenderly but clumsily tries to comfort her: isn't he worth more than ten sons? He loves her, but cannot fully understand her grief.

f.w: better to thee than ten sons

n: After the meal Hannah goes to pray. Eli the priest is sitting by the doorpost of the sanctuary — the chief priest and judge of Israel at the time.

f.g: Here the tabernacle complex at Shiloh, called a “temple” (palace of God).

n: In deep anguish Hannah takes her pain to the Lord in prayer and weeps freely. Her example shows that honest sorrow can be brought to God.
Hannah makes a vow: if God gives her a son, she will dedicate him to the Lord for life. No razor on his head echoes the Nazarite vow of special consecration.

f.w: there shall no razor come upon his head
f.g: A sign of the Nazarite vow of holiness.

n: As Hannah keeps praying, Eli watches her lips move.

f.g: watched, observed closely

n: Hannah prays silently, her lips moving without sound. People usually prayed aloud, so Eli wrongly assumes she is drunk.
Eli rebukes her harshly, telling her to stop drinking — a painful misunderstanding in her moment of greatest need.
Hannah respectfully corrects him: she is not drunk but heartbroken, pouring out her soul to the Lord.

f.g: beer or other fermented drink

n: She asks Eli not to think of her as a worthless woman; she has been speaking from great distress.

f.g: “Belial” means worthlessness; a “son” or “daughter of Belial” is a wicked or good-for-nothing person.

n: Eli realizes his mistake and blesses her, praying that God will grant her request. As the Lord's priest, his blessing carries authority.
Hannah humbly thanks Eli and leaves. She eats again and her face is no longer sad — she has left her burden with the Lord in faith, before seeing any answer.

f.w: her countenance was no more sad

n: The family worships and returns home to Ramah. Hannah conceives, and the text says the Lord “remembered” her — He had never forgotten her.

f.g: A Hebrew way of describing marital intimacy.

n: Hannah gives birth to a son and names him Samuel, explaining that she asked him of the Lord. His name is a lasting reminder that prayer was answered.

f.g: Possibly “name of God” or “heard of God”; Hannah connects it to the Hebrew word for “asked.”

n: The next year Elkanah's household goes to Shiloh for the annual sacrifice and to fulfill his vow.

f.g: Elkanah may have joined in Hannah's vow; a husband could confirm his wife's vows.

n: Hannah stays home until Samuel is weaned — perhaps two or three years in that culture — then plans to bring him to live permanently at the Lord's house.

f.g: In the ancient Near East children were often nursed until about age three.

n: Elkanah supports her decision and prays that the Lord will fulfill His word. Hannah nurses Samuel at home until he is weaned.

f.g: stay, wait

n: When the time comes, Hannah brings Samuel to Shiloh with a generous offering. The boy is still very young — her sacrifice is real.

f.g: young bulls; the Greek Septuagint reads “a three-year-old bull.”
a wineskin

n: They offer the sacrifice and present the child to Eli, who will raise him in the Lord's service.
Hannah reminds Eli that she is the woman he saw praying in that very place years earlier.

f.g: A polite oath: “as surely as you live.”

n: She testifies simply: she prayed for this child, and the Lord answered.
Hannah gives Samuel back to the Lord for his whole life, keeping her vow at great personal cost. Her faithfulness prepares a prophet who will guide all Israel.

f.g: The Hebrew is the same root as “asked” — Samuel was “asked” of the Lord and is now “given back” to Him.
